evidence.claim: Inconsistent definition of baseline for Connectivity Gain; text and figures contradict each other, making it unclear what baseline the gains are measured against.
evidence.excerpt: Section V.B defines 'Connectivity Gain' as the 'relative increase over a single-hop V2I baseline'. However, the y-axis of Figure 3 is labeled 'Mean 1-hop Connectivity Gain (%) vs Greedy'. The greedy SNR-based heuristic (defined in Section IV.D) and the single-hop V2I baseline are distinct strategies. This contradiction makes it unclear which baseline the gains in Section V.G and Figure 3 are actually being compared against.

judge_panel.reason: Section V.B defines Connectivity Gain as 'relative increase over a single-hop V2I baseline,' but Figure 3's y-axis is labeled 'Mean 1-hop Connectivity Gain (%) vs Greedy,' indicating gains are measured relative to the greedy SNR heuristic. These are distinct baselines, and the paper does not reconcile this discrepancy, making it genuinely unclear which baseline underpins the reported gains in Section V.G and Figure 3.

The paper defines the metric as "Connectivity Gain (relative increase over a single-hop V2I baseline)" (Sec. V.B), but Figure 3 is labeled "City-Aware 1-hop Connectivity Gain: L2O and MILP vs Greedy" with y-axis "Mean 1-hop Connectivity Gain (%) vs Greedy." Since Sec. V.G then states "Overall, across all regimes, L2O improves 1-hop connectivity in more than 97% of the evaluated snapshots," the manuscript uses both single-hop V2I and greedy as baselines without clearly reconciling them.

Section V.B explicitly defines Connectivity Gain as the 'relative increase over a single-hop V2I baseline', whereas Figure 3's y-axis is labeled 'Mean 1-hop Connectivity Gain (%) vs Greedy', confirming the contradiction raised by the reviewer.
